newsitem.title: FRANCE: Dollar helps French exports but growth doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Dollar helps French exports but growth doubts remain.

text.p: French companies are cashing in on a dollar-generated export boom, which is driving output forecasts higher and fuelling expectations of slight producer price rises, a quarterly industry survey showed on Wednesday.

The survey by national statistics institute INSEE showed that manufacturers expect demand to continue to rise in the third quarter at the same rate as in the second, with producer prices seen ticking up by 0.2 percent after a rise of 0.1 percent.
Analysts pointed to the sharp rise in bottlenecks since January and a stabilisation at higher capacity utilisation rates as a signal of an upturn in the business cycle.

"The survey was very positive," said Eric Chaney, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris. "I see domestic and foreign demand accelerating in both the second and third quarters. Another confirmation of the upturn is that bottlenecks have increased."
The export boom is being driven by the dollar, which has appreciated some 22 percent against the franc since January to around 6.38 francs per dollar.

But for some analysts, the main concern is internal demand, which is still lagging the export sector. Consumer spending fell a hefty 2.9 percent in June and was down 0.5 percent in the second quarter after a first quarter increase of 0.6 percent.
"Producer prices are picking up. We have probably reached the end of the period of disinflation but that does not mean we are beginning a period of inflation," said Eric Muller of UBS.

"The big factor in industrial production is external demand. We are a little bit afraid of seeing the same as in 1994 when external demand was strong but then we saw a blip in growth as there were no internal factors backing this up," said Caroline Newhouse Cohen of Louis Dreyfus Finance.
The survey also held out little hope for an improvement in France's record 12.6 percent unemployment rate. Employers merely see staff levels stabilising in the third quarter.

The Socialist-led government has made fighting unemployment its top priority and pledged to create 350,000 jobs for young people in the public sector over the coming several years as well as to push for a similar number of new jobs in the private sector.
Analysts say one factor undermining growth prospects has been an unwillingness to invest and say the parliamentary election which swept the left to power in June aggravated this phenomenon.

Muller said companies might still hold back on investment decisions until the details of the 1998 budget were known and also until the outcome of a government-sponsored conference starting in September on jobs, wages and the reduction of working hours.
Others were more optimistic on investment. "My interpretation is that there is not just an inventory kick but that capital spending is increasing in Europe and in France," said Chaney.

The previous centre-right government had forecast economic growth of at least 2.3 percent this year. Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's new left-wing coalition is banking on boosting consumer demand to help lift an economy which it says was damaged by the previous government's austerity drive.
